title: Mamdani’s not the first to try to bring cheap groceries to N.Y.C.
gist: Yglesias places Zohran Mamdani's municipal grocery plan in the lineage of Walmart's blocked 2004 attempt to enter New York City at Rego Park, and marshals research (DellaVigna-Gentzkow on uniform chain pricing, Basker on 6-12 percent price declines from Walmart entry, Handbury on poor households in rich cities) to argue that N.Y.C.'s high grocery prices stem from store mix rather than local price gouging. The blocker in both cases is the U.F.C.W.-led coordinated anti-Walmart campaign. (Paid post; text cuts off at 'The long war on Walmart'.)

insights.claim: Walmart, under CEO H. Lee Scott, announced its first New York City location in Rego Park, Queens in 2004 and ultimately failed to enter the city — making Zohran Mamdani far from the first actor to try to bring cheap groceries to N.Y.C.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: The historical precedent reframes the municipal-grocery debate: the obstacle to cheap groceries in N.Y.C. has been political, not commercial.
insights.quote: His name was H. Lee Scott
insights.locator: The most prominent attempt to do this

insights.claim: Rego Park was chosen as a proof of concept for a broader Walmart urban strategy, because success in a dense, subway-served, freeway-adjacent New York neighborhood would validate expansion into other traditionally laid-out cities.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Explains why urban-format retail entry has been repeatedly attempted and why the blocked N.Y.C. beachhead delayed a whole category of expansion.
insights.quote: So if Walmart could make it work in Rego Park, they’d expand to other N.Y.C. locations

insights.claim: Walmart's N.Y.C. push collided with a national coordinated campaign led by labor unions, especially the United Food and Commercial Workers, whose realistic aim was to halt Walmart expansion and protect U.F.C.W.-represented supermarkets.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Identifies the incumbent-protection mechanism that keeps N.Y.C. grocery prices high — and the same interest that any Mamdani plan must survive.
insights.quote: led by labor unions but especially by the United Food and Commercial Workers union

themes.theme: Why store mix, not local pricing, drives N.Y.C. prices

insights.claim: Research by Stefano DellaVigna and Matthew Gentzkow finds chain retailers very rarely practice location-specific price variation, so high N.Y.C. grocery prices are caused mainly by which stores operate there rather than by chains charging New Yorkers more.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Redirects the policy lever from price regulation to entry: fixing the store mix, not policing markups, is what would lower prices.
insights.quote: chain retailers very rarely practice location-specific price variation
insights.locator: Their logic essentially tracks what Mamdani

insights.claim: Emek Basker found in 2005 that Walmart's entry into a new market lowers average retail prices of grocery-type products by 6 to 12 percent.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A hard magnitude for the consumer-price effect of low-cost grocery entry, useful for evaluating any cheap-groceries policy claim.
insights.quote: average retail prices of grocery-type products fall by between 6 and 12 percent

insights.claim: Basker's later work with Michael Noel decomposes that effect: incumbent stores cut prices only about 1 percent, while Walmart's own prices being roughly 10 percent lower does most of the work — a pattern replicated in research on Walmart's entry into Mexico.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Implies a cheap-grocery entrant delivers savings mostly to its own shoppers, so scale and location of the new stores matter far more than competitive spillover.
insights.quote: existing stores drop prices by maybe 1 percent
insights.locator: Basker's later research with Michael Noel

insights.claim: Jessie Handbury's research finds poor households in affluent cities suffer significant welfare loss because the local retail mix is optimized for rich customers, which is why a thrift-focused broad-line retailer would disproportionately help low-income New Yorkers.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Gives the distributional case for cheap-grocery entry and identifies who actually captures the benefit.
insights.quote: poor people in affluent cities can experience significant welfare loss from being exposed to a retail mix that’s optimized for rich customers
insights.locator: This is especially important for low-income New Yorkers

themes.theme: Mamdani's plan judged on the evidence

insights.claim: Because location-specific chain pricing is rare, Mamdani's strategy of opening cheaper stores rather than regulating existing ones is the economically coherent lever — his logic essentially tracks Walmart's own 2004 logic.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A sympathetic-but-analytic read: the mechanism is sound, so execution and political resistance are the variables to watch, not the theory.
insights.quote: Thus the Mamdani strategy of trying to open cheaper stores makes sense.
insights.locator: Their logic essentially tracks what Mamdani
